stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: Marine biologists have long known that cleaner wrasses pick parasites off larger reef fish, but it has been unclear whether those larger "client" fish choose among cleaners. To find out, biologist Ana Ferreira filmed cleaning stations on a coral reef for six weeks. <u>Client fish that had watched a cleaner bite into another fish's skin instead of eating its parasites became far less likely to approach that cleaner afterward.</u> Ferreira concludes that client fish may keep track of individual cleaners' reputations.
choices: It explains the method Ferreira used to observe how client fish watched cleaners at the stations.
It presents an observation that helps answer the question raised in the first sentence of the text.
It challenges the long-held view that cleaner wrasses remove parasites from larger reef fish.
It states the text's conclusion that client fish keep track of the reputations of all reef cleaners.
explanation: The first sentence raises an open question: do client fish choose among cleaners? The second sentence describes how Ferreira set out to study it. The underlined sentence gives what she saw: clients avoided a cleaner after watching it bite another fish. That is a result, and it bears directly on the question from the first sentence. The last sentence then draws the conclusion. Choice B names the sentence's role and links it to the right part of the text.

A.why: You latched onto the word 'watched' and called the sentence a method. The method is in the sentence before it (filming cleaning stations for six weeks). The underlined sentence reports what the filming showed, so it is a result.

C.why: You got the relationship wrong. The text takes it as known that wrasses remove parasites and never questions that. The underlined sentence is about how clients respond to cleaners. It doesn't push back on that background fact.

D.why: You gave the underlined sentence the job of the last sentence, and you made the claim stronger too. The conclusion comes after the underlined sentence, and it says clients 'may' track 'individual cleaners' reputations.' Nothing in the text says clients track all reef cleaners.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: City planners have traditionally assumed that adding lanes to a congested road will ease traffic on it. Yet decades of data from widened highways suggest otherwise: congestion on such roads usually returns to its earlier level within five to ten years. <u>The new lanes draw drivers who had previously taken other routes, traveled at other hours, or skipped the trip entirely.</u> Transportation researchers call this effect induced demand, and many now argue that it should be weighed before any widening project is approved.
choices: It explains the method researchers used to track changes in drivers' routes and travel times.
It describes a pattern that helps account for why widening roads has not eased congestion.
It provides support for planners' traditional view that adding lanes reduces traffic on a road.
It states the text's recommendation that cities stop approving any new road-widening projects.
explanation: The text opens with an old belief (more lanes ease traffic) and then corrects it: congestion comes back within five to ten years. The underlined sentence tells you why it comes back. The new lanes pull in drivers who used to go another way, at another time, or not at all. Without this sentence you would know that widening fails but not how. Choice B names that explaining role and ties it to the right idea.

A.why: You matched the words 'routes' and 'hours' and called the sentence a method. The text never says how researchers gathered their data. The sentence explains why traffic comes back. It doesn't describe how anyone measured that.

C.why: You reversed the direction of the evidence. The 'Yet' tells you the text is arguing against the traditional view. The underlined sentence explains why new lanes fill up again, so it weakens that view.

D.why: You gave the underlined sentence the job of the last sentence and made the claim stronger too. The text says only that many researchers think induced demand 'should be weighed' before approving a project. It never says cities should stop approving widenings, and the underlined sentence makes no recommendation.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: Forecasters have long assumed that the lightning produced by a thunderstorm is concentrated near the storm's core, where updrafts are strongest. Yet when meteorologist Ana Ferreira mapped strikes from dozens of storms over the Brazilian plains, a different pattern emerged. <u>Nearly a third of the strikes she recorded landed more than 15 kilometers from a storm's center, beneath its trailing anvil cloud.</u> Ferreira argues that safety guidance based only on distance from the core may therefore underestimate the danger zone.
choices: It presents a finding that challenges the assumption described in the first sentence.
It explains the method Ferreira used to map lightning strikes across the plains.
It describes the conditions that make updrafts strongest near a storm's core.
It proposes a change to safety guidance that the final sentence then rejects.
explanation: The first sentence gives the old belief: lightning stays near the core. 'Yet' signals a correction, and the underlined sentence supplies the evidence: a third of strikes landed more than 15 kilometers away. Its job is to report a result that cuts against the assumption, and the last sentence builds on that result.

B.why: You matched 'strikes she recorded' to the word 'mapped' and called the sentence a method. The mapping is mentioned in the sentence before. The underlined sentence reports what the mapping found, so it is a result, not a method.

C.why: You picked up 'storm's center' and linked it to the updrafts in the first sentence. The underlined sentence is about strikes landing far from the core. It never explains updrafts, and it works against the core-focused view rather than describing it.

D.why: The underlined sentence proposes no guidance, and the final sentence doesn't reject anything. It draws on the finding to question existing guidance. You got both the role and the relationship wrong.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: It has long been unclear whether comets entering the inner solar system for the first time differ chemically from comets that have made many passes around the Sun. To find out, astronomer Kenji Hollis compared the gases released by twelve first-time visitors with those released by twenty frequent returners. <u>The first-time comets gave off nearly four times as much carbon monoxide, a compound that boils away quickly once a comet is warmed by sunlight.</u> Hollis concludes that repeated passes gradually strip comets of their most volatile ices.
choices: It describes how Hollis chose the comets that were included in his comparison.
It presents a result of Hollis's comparison that supports his final conclusion.
It defines a compound that astronomers use to identify comets on a first visit.
It raises a doubt about Hollis's conclusion that the final sentence resolves.
explanation: The text opens with a question, then describes Hollis's comparison (the method). The underlined sentence gives what the comparison found: first-time comets released far more carbon monoxide. The last sentence draws a conclusion from that result. So the underlined sentence is a finding that supports the conclusion.

A.why: This is the trap of calling a result a method. The sentence before the underlined one sets up the comparison. The underlined sentence reports what came out of it.

C.why: You latched onto the clause explaining what carbon monoxide does. That clause is a supporting detail, not the sentence's main job. The text also never says astronomers use the compound to identify first-time comets.

D.why: The underlined sentence backs Hollis's conclusion. Nothing in it casts doubt. You got the relationship backwards.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: Paleobotanists often estimate ancient temperatures from fossil leaves. <u>In living forests, the share of tree species with smooth-edged leaves rises steadily as average temperature increases.</u> Applying this relationship to a 50-million-year-old fossil bed in Wyoming, researcher Tomás Leal found that about 70 percent of its leaf types had smooth edges, a proportion found today only in forests where yearly temperatures average above 20°C. Leal infers that the region was once nearly subtropical.
choices: It states a general pattern that the rest of the text applies to fossil evidence.
It reports a finding from the Wyoming fossil bed that Leal examined directly.
It explains why paleobotanists have stopped relying on fossil leaves as clues.
It describes how smooth-edged leaves help trees survive in warmer climates.
explanation: The underlined sentence is the only one with no names, places, or numbers. It states a general rule about living forests. The next sentence opens with 'Applying this relationship,' and Leal then uses the rule on the Wyoming fossils. The underlined sentence lays down the pattern that the rest of the text puts to use.

B.why: You pointed to the wrong part of the text. The Wyoming finding (70 percent smooth-edged) comes in the next sentence. The underlined sentence describes living forests, not the fossil bed.

C.why: The first sentence says paleobotanists do rely on fossil leaves, and the underlined sentence gives the basis for doing so. Nothing suggests the method has been abandoned.

D.why: The sentence says only that smooth edges become more common as temperatures rise. It gives no reason or survival benefit. This is the content trap with an explanation the text never offers added on.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: Groundwater stored beneath deserts is often described as "fossil water," left over from wetter climates thousands of years ago and no longer replenished. In recent years, however, hydrologist Leila Mansour has questioned how complete that picture is. <u>Measuring chemical tracers in wells across southern Morocco, she found that some of the water had entered the aquifer within the past fifty years, likely carried down by rare flash floods.</u> Mansour cautions that this recharge is small but says it should be counted when limits on pumping are set.
choices: It provides evidence for Mansour's doubts about a common view of desert groundwater.
It explains why flash floods in southern Morocco have become more frequent recently.
It describes the chemical tracers hydrologists rely on to date very old groundwater.
It qualifies Mansour's claim by noting that the recharge she measured was small.
explanation: The first sentence gives the usual view: desert groundwater is ancient and not replenished. 'However' brings in Mansour's doubt. The underlined sentence backs that doubt with evidence: some of the water arrived within the past fifty years. Its role is supporting evidence for the challenge to the 'fossil water' view.

B.why: Flash floods come up only as the likely way water reached the aquifer. The text never says they are becoming more frequent. You built a claim the passage doesn't support.

C.why: This is the trap of matching words. 'Chemical tracers' appears in the sentence, but only as the tool behind the finding. The sentence reports what Mansour found, not how tracers work. Its point is also that some of the water is young, not old.

D.why: The caution that the recharge is small comes in the final sentence, not the underlined one. You gave the underlined sentence a role that belongs to another part of the text.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: Stories of a giant sea serpent told in Maine fishing villages were long assumed to have passed by word of mouth from one generation to the next. Folklorist Dana Whitcomb, however, found that the earliest known versions appeared in a regional newspaper in 1884. <u>Over the following decades, details from those printed accounts, such as the serpent's red mane and its habit of trailing boats at dusk, began turning up in stories that villagers told to interviewers.</u> Whitcomb argues that print, not only speech, shaped the tradition.
choices: It describes the features of the serpent that villagers found most frightening.
It presents evidence that folklorists used to argue the stories were purely oral.
It traces how printed details entered spoken tales, supporting Whitcomb's argument.
It explains the method Whitcomb used to locate the 1884 newspaper accounts.
explanation: The text starts with an old belief (the stories were purely oral), then corrects it with 'however': the earliest versions were printed. The underlined sentence goes further, showing details from the newspaper turning up later in what villagers said. That supports Whitcomb's closing claim that print shaped the tradition.

A.why: This is the content trap. The red mane and dusk trailing are examples of details that moved from print to speech. The text never says villagers found them the most frightening, and listing features isn't the sentence's job.

B.why: The sentence works against the purely oral view, not for it. You got the relationship backwards and credited the evidence to the side it undercuts.

D.why: You took a result for a method. The sentence says nothing about how Whitcomb found the newspaper. It reports what happened to the printed details afterward.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: Nutritionists long treated the cholesterol in eggs as a major driver of cholesterol in the blood. To test that assumption, researchers assigned 48 adults to eat either two eggs or an egg-free breakfast every morning for twelve weeks. <u>At the end of the trial, average blood cholesterol in the two groups differed by less than 2 percent.</u> Results like these help explain why several national dietary guidelines have since dropped their daily cholesterol limits.
choices: It presents a result that casts doubt on the long-held view described in the first sentence.
It describes the method the researchers used to divide the adults into two breakfast groups.
It explains why several national guidelines removed their limits on daily cholesterol intake.
It shows that eating eggs every day has no effect on any measure of a person's health.
explanation: Cover the underlined sentence and see what goes missing. The first sentence states an old belief and the second sets up a test of it. Without the underlined sentence, the test has no outcome. The sentence reports what the trial found: almost no difference between the groups. That is a result, and it counts against the belief that eggs drive blood cholesterol up.

B.why: You matched the words 'two groups' and called the sentence a method. The groups were set up in the sentence before. The underlined sentence reports what happened at the end of the trial, so it is a result.

C.why: You gave the underlined sentence the job of the sentence after it. The final sentence is the one that links results like these to the guidelines. The underlined sentence only reports what the trial found.

D.why: The trial measured only blood cholesterol, in 48 adults over twelve weeks. 'No effect on any measure of health' claims far more than one small result can support.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: Fever is usually treated as a symptom to be brought down as quickly as possible. Some immunologists, however, argue that the rise in temperature is itself part of the body's defense. <u>Many immune processes work faster within a narrow band of elevated heat.</u> In laboratory cultures warmed to 39°C, for instance, human T cells multiplied nearly twice as quickly as matching cultures kept at 37°C, and neutrophils moved toward bacteria more rapidly.
choices: It states a general principle that the laboratory observations in the next sentence illustrate.
It reports a laboratory result showing that T cells multiplied faster in warmer cultures.
It defines the term "fever" in the way the rest of the text goes on to use it.
It establishes that a fever should never be lowered with medication during an illness.
explanation: Notice that the underlined sentence is the only one with no numbers and no named cells. It states a broad rule: immune processes speed up with some extra heat. The next sentence opens with 'for instance' and gives specific cases, T cells and neutrophils at 39°C. So the underlined sentence is the general principle, and the concrete findings that follow illustrate it.

B.why: You took the role from the next sentence. The T cells and the 39°C cultures appear only after 'for instance'. The underlined sentence is the general claim those results illustrate, not a result itself.

C.why: The underlined sentence never says what a fever is. It makes a claim about how immune processes respond to heat. Calling it a definition misses the job it does in the argument.

D.why: The text says some immunologists see fever as part of the defense. It never goes as far as a rule about medication. 'Never be lowered' is a claim the passage does not make.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: It has long been unclear whether the blue in many early-nineteenth-century Japanese woodblock prints came from imported Prussian blue or from plant-based indigo. To find out, conservator Lena Ostrowski examined 30 prints with a handheld spectrometer, a device that identifies pigments from the light they reflect without removing any paint. <u>Prints made after 1829 consistently showed the signature of Prussian blue, while earlier ones showed indigo.</u> The shift suggests that workshops adopted the imported pigment soon after it became affordable.
choices: It presents the finding that answers the question raised at the start of the text.
It explains how the spectrometer identified pigments without damaging the prints.
It offers a reason that print workshops switched from one blue pigment to another.
It proves that no workshop used indigo in any print it made after the year 1829.
explanation: Sketch the structure: open question (which blue?), then method (the spectrometer), then the underlined sentence, then an interpretation. The underlined sentence tells you what the examination found, which pigment shows up in which period. That finding is the answer to the question raised in the first sentence.

B.why: You called a result a method, which is this subtype's trap. The spectrometer and how it works are described in the sentence before. The underlined sentence reports what that method turned up.

C.why: The reason, that workshops adopted the pigment once it was affordable, comes in the last sentence. The underlined sentence reports the pattern in the prints but does not explain it.

D.why: The pattern comes from 30 prints. 'Consistently' describes that sample, not every print any workshop ever made. 'Proves that no workshop' stretches a sample into a universal claim.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: Economists have traditionally assumed that raising a city's minimum wage pushes employers to cut hours for their lowest-paid workers. Economist Lena Okafor tested this by comparing restaurants in two neighboring towns, only one of which had raised its wage floor. <u>A year later, average weekly hours for entry-level staff in the two towns differed by less than one hour.</u> Okafor argues that, at least for modest increases, any reduction in hours may be far smaller than economists have expected.
choices: It describes how Okafor selected the two towns whose restaurants she compared in her study.
It presents a finding that casts doubt on the assumption described in the first sentence.
It confirms that raising a minimum wage leads employers to cut their workers' weekly hours.
It shows that raising a minimum wage has no effect on employment in any industry at all.
explanation: Sketch the passage: old belief (higher wage floors mean fewer hours), then the study, then the underlined result, then the conclusion. Cover the underlined sentence and the conclusion has no support. The sentence reports what Okafor found: hours in the two towns barely differed. That result works against the traditional assumption in the first sentence, which is what choice B says.

A.why: You called a result a method. The study design (two neighboring towns, only one with a raise) is in the sentence before. The underlined sentence tells you what the comparison showed a year later.

C.why: You reversed the relationship. A gap of less than one hour is evidence against the idea that employers cut hours. It doesn't support it, and Okafor's conclusion questions the assumption too.

D.why: You stretched the finding too far. The study covers entry-level restaurant staff in two towns, and Okafor limits her claim to modest increases. Nothing in the text supports a claim about every industry.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: Farmers who plant clover between rows of corn hope it will add nitrogen to the soil, but it has been unclear whether the clover also takes water the corn needs during dry summers. Agronomist Tomás Reyes grew corn with and without clover through two drought years. <u>In both years, corn grown with clover yielded about 4 percent less grain than corn grown alone, a much smaller gap than the 20 percent loss many growers had feared.</u> Reyes suggests that clover's cost to corn in dry years may be modest.
choices: It explains the method Reyes used to compare corn grown with and without clover in drought years.
It reports a result that addresses the uncertainty raised in the first sentence of the text.
It shows that clover adds more nitrogen to the soil in drought years than it does in wet years.
It indicates that clover does not take any of the water that corn needs during dry summers.
explanation: The first sentence raises an open question: does clover take water the corn needs in dry summers? The second sentence sets up Reyes's trial. The underlined sentence gives the outcome: a small yield gap, much smaller than growers feared. That is a result that answers the opening question, and Reyes's suggestion in the last sentence is built on it. Choice B names that role and links it to the right part of the text.

A.why: You picked up the words 'with clover' and 'grown alone' and treated the sentence as the method. The method (growing corn with and without clover through two drought years) comes in the sentence before. The underlined sentence gives the numbers that trial produced.

C.why: You brought in a claim the text never makes. Nitrogen comes up only as farmers' hope in the first sentence, and the study measures grain yield in drought years only. Nothing compares nitrogen across wet and dry years.

D.why: You turned 'a smaller gap' into 'no gap.' Corn with clover still yielded about 4 percent less, so the text suggests some cost. Reyes calls that cost modest. He never says it is zero.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: In eighteenth-century Japan, a woodblock print passed through several hands: a designer drew the image, a carver cut it into cherry wood, and a printer inked and pressed each sheet. Collectors have usually credited the designer alone. <u>Yet when historian Mariko Sato compared early and late impressions from the same blocks, she found that the colors changed far more from one edition to the next than the drawn lines did.</u> Sato argues that printers, who chose those colors, shaped these works more than their anonymity suggests.
choices: It introduces evidence that complicates the collecting practice described in the previous sentence.
It explains how a carver transferred a designer's drawing onto a block of cherry wood for printing.
It supports collectors' long-standing view that the designer alone determined how a print looked.
It proves that printers, rather than designers, were the true creators of most woodblock prints.
explanation: Sketch the structure: background on who made a print, the usual practice (credit only the designer), then 'Yet' and Sato's comparison, then her argument. The underlined sentence comes right after the pivot. The difference it reports, colors varying far more than lines, is evidence that someone besides the designer shaped the print. That complicates crediting the designer alone, which is what choice A says.

B.why: You described the first sentence, not the underlined one. Carving is mentioned only as background. The underlined sentence is about comparing impressions from different editions, and it says nothing about how a carver worked.

C.why: You missed the 'Yet.' It marks a turn against the collectors' view. If colors changed between editions while the designer's lines stayed the same, the designer did not decide everything about how a print looked.

D.why: You made the claim too strong. Sato says printers shaped the works more than people have recognized. She doesn't say they replaced designers as the creators, and 'proves' is stronger than one comparison of impressions can support.

stem: Which choice does NOT accurately describe the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: Historians have long described the eighteenth-century calico trade out of western India as a story of finished cloth flowing west to European buyers. Historian Priya Raman's study of merchant records from the port of Surat complicates that account. <u>Ledgers kept by Surat traders between 1740 and 1760 list more shipments of raw indigo and madder root to Southeast Asia than of printed cotton to Europe.</u> For these traders, at least, dyestuffs rather than cloth appear to have been the more valuable export.
choices: It provides evidence that complicates the account of the trade given in the first sentence.
It explains the method Raman used to date the ledgers kept by the Surat traders.
It offers an example of the merchant records mentioned in the preceding sentence.
It presents the specific data on which the final sentence's conclusion is based.
explanation: Sketch the passage first: an old view (cloth flowed west), a pivot (Raman's records complicate it), the underlined evidence (more dyestuff shipments than cloth), then a conclusion (dyestuffs mattered more). The underlined sentence reports what the ledgers show. It is a result, not a method, and it never says how the ledgers were dated. Choice B borrows the words 'ledgers' and 'Surat traders' but gives the sentence the wrong role, so it is the one description that fails.

A.why: You may have thought 'complicates' was too strong a verb. The text itself says Raman's records complicate the cloth-flowing-west account, and the underlined ledger figures are what do that work. The description is accurate, so it can't be the answer to a NOT question.

C.why: You may have decided this choice points to the wrong part of the text. The preceding sentence mentions Raman's study of merchant records, and the underlined ledgers are one of those records. The link is correct, so this description holds.

D.why: You may have read the final sentence as a separate point rather than one drawn from the underlined sentence. 'Dyestuffs rather than cloth' rests directly on the shipment counts in the ledgers, so this description is true.

stem: Which choice does NOT accurately describe the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: Forecasters have generally treated hail size as a product of a storm's updraft strength alone. Meteorologist Tomás Ibarra set out to test whether the moisture of the air feeding a storm also matters. <u>Comparing radar records from 212 summer storms on the Great Plains, he found that storms with similar updraft speeds produced markedly larger hailstones when the low-level air was humid.</u> Ibarra argues that forecasts of hail size should therefore weigh humidity alongside updraft strength.
choices: It reports the result of the comparison Ibarra made to address his question.
It presents a finding that qualifies the view described in the first sentence.
It supplies the basis for the recommendation Ibarra makes in the final sentence.
It refutes the idea that updraft strength has any effect on the size of hail.
explanation: The passage runs from an assumption (updrafts alone set hail size) to a question (does moisture matter too?), then the underlined result (at similar updraft speeds, humid air gave larger hail), then a recommendation. The finding adds humidity as a second factor. It holds updraft speed steady and doesn't deny that updrafts matter; the final sentence even keeps updraft strength in the forecast. 'Refutes' is too strong a verb, so choice D is the description that fails.

A.why: You may have taken the underlined sentence for a description of the question rather than its answer. It begins with the comparison Ibarra made and ends with what he found, which is a result that answers the question raised in the second sentence. The description is accurate.

B.why: You may have thought the finding contradicts the first sentence outright, which would make 'qualifies' too weak. The finding limits the 'updraft strength alone' view by adding humidity without dismissing updrafts, and that is exactly what qualifying means. The description is true.

C.why: You may have thought the final sentence stands on its own. It begins with 'therefore,' which shows it draws on the underlined finding. The description correctly names the part of the text the sentence supports.

stem: Which choice does NOT accurately describe the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus: Off the coast of Baja California, marine biologist Leah Okafor tagged juvenile yellowtail that had hatched near a single kelp bed. Years later, most of the tagged fish that were recaptured had returned to spawn within a few kilometers of that bed. <u>Such findings suggest that a fish's earliest surroundings can shape where it breeds long after it has left them.</u> Okafor now plans to test whether the pattern holds for species whose larvae drift much farther from home.
choices: It presents a finding that contradicts the recapture results reported in the preceding sentence.
It states a general principle that the tagging results described before it illustrate.
It draws a broader conclusion from the specific observations of the tagged yellowtail.
It offers the idea whose reach Okafor plans to test in the study the final sentence describes.
explanation: The underlined sentence is the abstract one among the specifics: no place names and no species, just a broad rule that early surroundings can shape later breeding sites. It grows directly out of the recapture results and agrees with them. It doesn't contradict them. Choice A gets that relationship backward, so it is the one description that fails.

B.why: You may have thought the principle comes before its example, so 'described before it' seemed to point the wrong way. Here the specific tagging results come first and the rule follows. They illustrate the rule, and the description is accurate.

C.why: You may have thought calling the sentence a 'broader conclusion' claims more than the passage supports. 'Such findings suggest' signals a generalization from the yellowtail data to fish in general, which is what this choice says. It is true.

D.why: You may have read the final sentence as introducing a new topic. 'The pattern' Okafor plans to test is the principle stated in the underlined sentence, now applied to species that drift farther. The description is correct.
